oneSentence: Data governance is the set of rules, roles and checks that control how data is collected, stored, used, shared and corrected over time.
plainExplanation:
Data governance is about making sure data is handled in a controlled, accountable way. It covers who may collect it, who may change it, what quality standard it should meet, how long it should be kept, and what records should exist about it. Those records are often called metadata, meaning information about the data, such as source, date and meaning.

What goes in? Many kinds of data, from spreadsheets and survey answers to documents and sensor records. Also important are the rules, roles and processes around that data. For example, one team may own a dataset, another may use it, and a named steward may check whether definitions stay consistent.

What happens? The organisation sets policies, assigns responsibilities, defines common terms, checks quality, manages access, and tracks changes. It also decides how data may be shared, archived or deleted. If problems appear, such as missing values or unclear labels, governance provides a process for fixing them and recording what changed.

What comes out is not new data by itself, but a more reliable data environment. People can see where data came from, whether it is suitable for a task, and what limits apply. That makes analysis, reporting and AI work safer and more consistent.

Data governance is often confused with privacy or AI governance. Privacy focuses on protecting personal data and people’s rights. AI governance is broader and covers the design, use and oversight of AI systems. Data governance is one part of both, but it also applies to non-AI uses of data.

everydayAnalogy.title: Reviewing practice exam results fairly
everydayAnalogy.story: A school runs a practice examination for 300 students. Before teachers compare results across classes, they agree on one marking guide, one file format, and one rule for how to record absent students. A coordinator checks that names are written the same way, late score changes are logged, and only authorised staff can open the full file. Because of those rules, the head teacher can compare trends without mixing up students, subjects or score scales.

mapping.analogyElement: coordinator checking names and logged changes
mapping.aiElement: data stewardship, quality control and audit trail

mapping.analogyElement: only authorised staff can open the full file
mapping.aiElement: access control and responsible data use

everydayAnalogy.limitation: An exam file is simpler than most real data environments. In organisations, data often comes from many systems at once, changes continuously, and may cross legal or geographic boundaries. Governance also covers retention, sharing, deletion and documentation over time, not just one review meeting.

visual.title: How data governance turns messy data handling into controlled use
visual.learningObjective: After viewing, the reader should be able to describe data governance as an ordered process of setting rules, assigning roles, checking quality and controlling use over time.
visual.description: A left-to-right step diagram with five connected boxes. Each box shows one stage in governing data, from setting purpose and rules to monitoring use and correcting problems. Read in order to see how raw data handling becomes documented, accountable and reusable.

steps.label: 1. Set purpose and rules
steps.explanation: Define why the data is being kept or used, what standards apply, and what is not allowed.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a box with a document icon and short labels: purpose, definitions, retention, sharing rules.

steps.label: 2. Assign roles
steps.explanation: Name who owns the dataset, who maintains it, who may use it, and who approves changes.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a box with four person icons labelled owner, steward, user, approver.

steps.label: 3. Check and document
steps.explanation: Record source, meaning and dates, then test for missing, inconsistent or outdated entries.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a box with a table icon and side tags reading source, date, definition, quality check.

steps.label: 4. Control access and use
steps.explanation: Allow only appropriate access, apply safeguards, and make sure use matches the agreed purpose.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a box with a lock over a dataset and a small badge saying approved use only.

steps.label: 5. Monitor and improve
steps.explanation: Track changes, log issues, review compliance, and update rules when data or needs change.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a box with a checklist and circular arrow, plus a small issue log panel.

visual.interaction: Clicking a step highlights it and reveals a short example of that stage, while keeping the full sequence visible.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram presents five ordered stages of data governance. First, an organisation sets the purpose for a dataset and writes rules on definitions, retention and sharing. Second, it assigns roles such as owner, steward, user and approver. Third, it documents where the data came from, what fields mean and when records were updated, then checks for missing or inconsistent entries. Fourth, it controls who may access or use the data and for what approved purpose. Fifth, it monitors changes, logs issues and improves the rules over time. The main message is that trustworthy data use comes from repeated management, not from collecting data alone.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static five-box horizontal diagram with arrows between boxes. The same labels and examples appear without animation or highlighting.

workedExample.scenario: A regional public health team wants one monthly dashboard from clinic reports sent by 12 districts.
workedExample.input: 12 spreadsheets with different column names, mixed date formats, and some blank values for patient age group.
process: The team writes a data standard: use one date format, one list of district names, and fixed age-group labels.
A data steward is assigned to receive files, rename columns, and record the source and submission date for each file.
Quality checks flag 18 blank age-group cells, 7 impossible dates, and 2 duplicate district submissions.
The steward sends questions back to districts, corrects confirmed errors, and logs each change in a change record.
Only the approved dashboard team can access the combined file, while a wider group sees only aggregated totals.
workedExample.result: The dashboard is produced on time with consistent district names and documented corrections, and users can see which fields are complete enough for comparison and which have limits.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN office is reviewing programme monitoring data from field partners to prepare an annual results summary.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Data governance helps the office agree on indicator definitions, document sources, assign who can edit the master dataset, and check whether partner reports are complete and comparable before analysis.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not upload personal, confidential, survivor, witness, security-sensitive or other protection-sensitive monitoring data to an unapproved public AI service; use approved systems, minimise personal data, and keep human oversight over access and correction decisions.

whyItMatters: Non-specialists make decisions from data all the time: budgets, programme changes, risk reviews and public reporting. If the data is poorly governed, numbers may look precise while actually meaning different things in different files, coming from unknown sources, or being used beyond their original purpose. Good data governance does not guarantee truth, but it makes data more traceable, consistent and accountable. That helps leaders ask better questions, spot weak evidence earlier, reduce legal and operational risk, and avoid building AI or analytics on a shaky foundation.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Data governance only matters for large technology companies.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Any organisation that relies on data can face confusion about definitions, access, quality or retention. A small programme team with three spreadsheets can still make poor decisions if one file counts households and another counts individuals without saying so.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Data governance means locking data away so nobody can use it.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The aim is controlled and appropriate use, not blanket restriction. Good governance often makes data easier to use because people know what it means, who approves access and what limits apply.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If data is accurate today, governance is finished.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Data changes over time. Staff move, collection methods change, systems are updated and new uses appear. Governance includes ongoing monitoring, change logs and review, not a one-time clean-up.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Data governance is the same as privacy.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Privacy is one important part when personal data is involved, but governance is broader. It also covers quality, documentation, ownership, retention, access, interoperability and appropriate use, including for non-personal data.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Data governance is the organised way an institution makes sure data is handled properly: clear rules, clear responsibilities, careful access and regular checks.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Data governance is the framework of policies, roles, standards, controls and review processes used to manage data across its lifecycle. It covers data ownership, stewardship, metadata, quality management, access control, retention, lineage or traceability, issue resolution and change management. Its goal is to make data usable, consistent, compliant and accountable across collection, storage, sharing, analysis and deletion. In practice, it links business rules with operational processes so people can tell what a dataset represents, where it came from, what constraints apply, and whether it is fit for a particular use.

keyTakeaway: Good data governance does not create better decisions by magic, but it makes the evidence behind decisions clearer, safer and easier to trust.

quickCheck.question: Which example best shows data governance rather than just data collection?
options: A team gathers more survey responses than last year.
A manager asks for a colourful dashboard by Friday.
An office sets standard indicator definitions, assigns a data steward, logs corrections and limits access by role.
A model produces a summary from a spreadsheet.
quickCheck.explanation: Data governance is about the rules, responsibilities and controls around data. Standard definitions, named stewardship, change logs and role-based access are all governance mechanisms. The other options may involve data, but they do not show how its handling is being governed.
